quote: Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.
speaker: Jack Swigert, Command Module Pilot, Apollo 13
source_title: Apollo 13 air-to-ground voice transcript
context_before: A bang and a shudder aboard the spacecraft after a routine cryo stir. Mission Control has just seen the telemetry twitch.
context_after: CapCom asks them to say again; Lovell repeats it and adds the Main B Bus Undervolt.
cultural_background: 13 April 1970. The most quoted sentence in spaceflight, and almost always quoted wrong — the film made it 'Houston, we have a problem', present tense, and that is the version Americans say. The real line is past tense and was spoken by Swigert, not Lovell.
why_it_lands: Total calm about a catastrophe, opened with 'Okay'. It is also a useful correction gag: the famous version is not what was said.
licence_note: NASA mission audio is a US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105, and usable commercially. The NASA insignia and logo are separately restricted — do not put them on screen.
topics: how professionals talk when it goes wrong
verification_note: Time anchor comes from the transcript page itself: the Spacelog URL is keyed to 02:07:55:19 elapsed (055:55:19 GET), and a second source independently places the transmission at 055:55:20. quote: Apollo 12, Houston. Try SCE to Auxiliary. Over.
speaker: CapCom Gerald Carr, relaying EECOM John Aaron
source_title: Apollo 12 air-to-ground voice transcript, lightning strike on ascent
context_before: Lightning has struck the vehicle twice in the first minute of flight. Every caution light in the spacecraft is lit and the telemetry has turned to garbage.
context_after: At 000:01:50 Conrad answers 'SCE to Aux'; Alan Bean finds the switch and the data comes back.
cultural_background: 14 November 1969. A 24-year-old flight controller recognised the garbled telemetry pattern from a simulation a year earlier and called an obscure switch nobody else in the room recognised. 'SCE to AUX' is engineering folklore in the US — the standard example of deep expertise paying off in four words.
why_it_lands: Four syllables of pure jargon that saved a Moon mission. Works standalone as absurd-sounding technical speech; richer if the narration explains what it meant. Pair it with the reply for a two-beat cut.
licence_note: NASA mission audio, 17 U.S.C. 105. Insignia restricted separately.
topics: the person who knew the one thing
verification_note: The Apollo Flight Journal page states both times: Carr's transmission at 000:01:36 and Conrad's reply at 000:01:50, mission elapsed time. Not an offset into a specific audio file.

quote: Flight controllers here looking very carefully at the situation. Obviously a major malfunction.

context_before: Routine ascent commentary. Seventy-three seconds after liftoff the vehicle breaks up; forty-one seconds of silence follow.

cultural_background: 28 January 1986. Challenger broke up on live television with a schoolteacher aboard, watched in classrooms across the country. Nesbitt's phrase became the title of books and documentaries and is the American shorthand for institutional language failing to meet a moment.
why_it_lands: Not a joke and must never be cut as one. It lands as the extreme case of the register this channel plays with: seven people have died and the official voice reaches for 'malfunction'. Usable only where the narration is about how institutions speak, and only with the weight left in.
